newsitem.title: UK: Britain's Labour vows to crack down on lottery operator.
newsitem.headline: Britain's Labour vows to crack down on lottery operator.

text.p: Britain's opposition Labour Party vowed on Wednesday to end the hefty profits generated by national lottery operator Camelot.

"When Camelot's current contract runs out in November 2001, Labour will seek a competitive, efficient, not-for-profit operator to ensure that the maximum sums go to good causes," the party, which is leading opinion polls ahead of expected to take power in the May 1 election, said in a document on the lottery.

National heritage spokesman Jack Cunningham told a news conference that Camelot was cashing in on its monopoly status under its seven-year licence. "People are angry that a private monopoly makes more than one million pounds ($1.6 million) per week profits on their lottery money," he said.

The national lottery, launched in November 1994, has proved hugely popular with Britons. Millions tune in to watch the draw live on television and Camelot have recently introduced a second, midweek game. However, Camelot, a consortium owned by five companies, came under fire last June when it announced pre-tax profits in its first full year of 77.5 million pounds.
Criticism grew when it emerged that Camelot chief executive Tim Holley had hit the jackpot with an annual pay package of 385,000 pounds -- including a 123,000 pound bonus.

Camelot points out that its profit after tax stands at less than one percent of turnover. It also notes it has now raised some 3.15 billion pounds for good causes -- arts, sports, charities, heritage and special millennium projects.
Labour said it planned to use the proceeds from the midweek draw to create a one billion pound fund for education and health projects.

A Camelot spokeswoman tried to play down the differences with Labour. "We're happy to work with the government of the day and will continue to operate the national lottery in accordance with parliament's wishes," she said.
Camelot is owned by Cadbury Schweppes Plc, De La Rue Plc, GTECH UK, Racal Electronics and ICL. The first four have 22.5 percent stakes while Fujitsu-owned ICL has the remaining 10 percent.
